title: Why Diffusion Models Don t Memorize:  The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regul

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments, Eq. (6) and definition of the memorization fraction
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equation (6) states that an individual generated sample x_tau is memorized if E_{x_tau}[||x_tau-a^{mu_1}||/||x_tau-a^{mu_2}||] < k. An expectation over generated samples is a model-level quantity, not a property of an individual sample. If interpreted literally, every sample would receive the same classification and a nontrivial fraction f_mem could not be computed. The standard nearest/second-nearest-neighbor criterion is the per-sample ratio without E_{x_tau}; the displayed equation and prose are inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments, 'Role of training set size on the learning dynamics,' discussion of Fig. 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper reports the central FID/memorization curves only 'after excluding runs where early stopping failed to improve FID by more than 15%, resulting in reduced variance but biased estimates.' Excluding runs based on the measured outcome selectively removes failures and biases the reported FID and apparent timing of generalization. The subsequent claims that all dynamics exhibit two phases and that tau_gen is independent of n are therefore not supported by the selected data unless all runs and the exclusion analysis are reported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments, Fig. 2 inset and tau_mem scaling claim
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The asserted collapse is obtained after normalizing each curve by its own f_mem(tau_max), while tau_max differs substantially across runs ('one to four million SGD steps'). This quantity is not an estimated asymptotic memorization fraction, and runs stopped earlier can have a substantially different denominator. Such self-normalization can alter apparent transition locations; it cannot by itself establish tau_mem proportional to n without showing saturation, common stopping times, unnormalized curves, and uncertainty for fitted transition times.

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments, subsection 'Memorization is not due to data repetition'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The section concludes that the effect 'confirms' a fundamental n-dependent loss-landscape change rather than data repetition, but immediately admits that 'alternative experiments with different batch sizes and update rules produce conflicting results, leaving the exact cause of memorization delay open.' Conflicting, unspecified experiments cannot support the claimed causal conclusion. Moreover, under the stated fixed-batch protocol B=min(n,512), at a fixed number of updates each example is processed approximately tau B/n times, which is explicitly not equal across n for n>512.

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments, final paragraph of 'Effect of the model capacity'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper first defines the phase boundary as 'the smallest n such that f_mem(tau)=0,' consistent with memorization decreasing as n grows. It later says it estimates n^*(p) by measuring 'the largest n(tau) yielding f_mem approximately 0.' These are opposite definitions. Given the paper's own monotonic narrative, the largest n with zero measured memorization is merely the largest tested n, not the transition threshold, so the claimed estimate of n^*(p) is not logically defined.

The boundaries are defined by f_mem(tau)=0 using a finite sample of generated images, but no detection limit or confidence-bound criterion is specified. Observing zero events only provides an upper bound on the memorization rate; it does not demonstrate that a model 'generalize[s] perfectly' or identify a sharp zero-memorization boundary. This is especially consequential because the stated bootstrap intervals may be underestimated and the threshold is used to infer an asymptotic architectural-regularization phase diagram.

The paper writes that eigenvalue timescales obey 'tau^{-1} = psi_p/(Delta_t lambda_min).' This is the inverse of the relaxation rate implied by Eq. (10). Since Eq. (10) contains the matrix factor Delta_t U/psi_p, a mode of U with eigenvalue lambda relaxes at rate Delta_t lambda/psi_p and has time tau=psi_p/(Delta_t lambda). The following sentence uses the latter expression for tau_mem, contradicting the preceding displayed relation.

The assumptions permit an activation with 'non-square-integrable terms,' while U and the quantities v_t^2 and s_t^2 explicitly require finite Gaussian second moments of sigma, including E[sigma(...)^2]. If sigma is not square-integrable under the relevant Gaussian input, these expectations and the entries/eigenvalue distribution of U need not exist. Theorems 3.1--3.2 therefore cannot follow under the stated assumptions without additional integrability conditions.

The text labels the result a theorem with proofs in the supplement, but says its alternative derivation is 'using the replica method' and expressly characterizes that method as 'a heuristic method.' A replica calculation can provide a non-rigorous prediction, but is not a proof of a theorem under the unusually broad stated assumptions (including heavy-tailed data and potentially unbounded covariance spectrum). The result must either be presented as heuristic or supported by a non-replica proof with assumptions sufficient for the claimed universality.

The abstract and main narrative present tau_mem increasing linearly with n as a central finding supported by both experiments and theory. The theoretical section instead states that in the overparameterized regime tau_mem 'exhibits a more complex dependence on both psi_n and the noise level Delta_t, and may scale sublinearly with n under varying noise schedules.' Thus the theory as described does not establish the paper's broad linear-in-n claim; the claim needs to be restricted to the tested fixed-noise/fixed-protocol setting and distinguished from the theoretical result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference [12] and all claims attributed to [12]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [12] is listed as 'Alias, J., Smith, T., and Doe, J. (2025). Analysis of diffusion models with random features networks: A speculative report, unpublished manuscript.' The placeholder-like author names and description do not constitute a verifiable scholarly source, yet the paper repeatedly treats it as an established prior analysis, including claims that it computed asymptotic losses and established an architectural threshold. These assertions require a real, retrievable citation or an independent derivation in this paper.

The manuscript attributes a relevant derivation to 'George et al. (2025),' but no George et al. work appears anywhere in the reference list. This is an uncitable attribution at the point where the paper motivates its spectral theorem and must be corrected with a complete, verifiable reference.

predicted_errors.error_location: Experiments and Method, repeated references to Supplemental Material
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The supplied document is identified as the full paper, but essential information is deferred to absent supplemental sections: the numerical setup (SM A), Adam experiments (SM A.3 and D), synthetic/conditional experiments (SM B), theorem proofs and precise assumptions (SM C), and RF numerical details (SM D). The main text does not provide learning rate, momentum, diffusion-time sampling/training weighting, augmentation/preprocessing, DDIM settings, run counts per condition, or the missing proofs. The central empirical and theoretical results consequently are not reproducible or auditable from the paper as provided.
